short: The purification of the self: the work of clearing the heart of what spoils it.
long: The Qur'an says the one who purifies the soul has succeeded (Qur'an 91:9), and lists purifying people among the tasks the Prophet peace be upon him was sent with (Qur'an 62:2). The subject covers both halves of the job: removing what is blameworthy, such as envy and arrogance, and planting what is praiseworthy, such as sincerity and gratitude. It is a discipline with a syllabus, not a mood, and it belongs to every Muslim rather than to one group.

short: The heart: in the Qur'an the seat of understanding and intention, not the organ alone.
long: The Qur'an speaks of a sound heart brought to Allah (Qur'an 26:89), of hearts that are sealed, and of hearts covered by rust from what they earned (Qur'an 83:14). The Prophet peace be upon him said there is a morsel of flesh in the body which, if it is sound, makes the whole body sound, and it is the heart, in Bukhari and Muslim. Classical writers describe it in three states: sound, sick, and dead. This is why the science of the heart is treated as a discipline and not a mood.

short: An alert, careful awareness of Allah that keeps a person away from what harms them.
long: The root means to guard or to shield, and carries the sense of putting something between yourself and danger. The Qur'an calls it the best provision for the journey (Qur'an 2:197), and the Prophet peace be upon him pointed to his chest three times and said taqwa is here, in a report collected by Muslim. It is not fear alone, and it is not a personality type. It is caution kept awake.

short: Doing an act for Allah alone, with no eye on who else is watching.
long: The word means to make something pure, with nothing mixed into it. The Qur'an says people were commanded only to worship Allah, sincerely devoting religion to Him (Qur'an 98:5), and the Prophet peace be upon him said actions are only by intentions, in Bukhari and Muslim. Ikhlas is not a feeling you generate before an act. It is what is left of the act when the praise does not arrive.

short: Performing worship so that people will see it, which empties the act of its reward.
long: The word comes from seeing, and its close cousin sum'ah is doing something so that people will hear of it. The Qur'an condemns those who pray only to be seen (Qur'an 107:6), and the Prophet peace be upon him called showing off the lesser shirk, in a report from Imam Ahmad. Being pleased that someone noticed a good deed is not riya. Riya is when being noticed was the reason you did it.

short: Truthfulness: that your words, your intentions and your actions all report the same thing.
long: The Qur'an tells the believers to be with the truthful (Qur'an 9:119), and the Prophet peace be upon him said truthfulness leads to righteousness and righteousness leads to Paradise, in Bukhari and Muslim. Writers on the heart use sidq more widely than honest speech: a truthful hope, a truthful repentance, a truthful claim to love Allah. In that sense its opposite is not only lying but posing.

short: Holding yourself steady under what is hard, without complaint to creation and without giving up.
long: The root means to restrain or to confine. Scholars usually give it three fields: steadiness in obeying Allah, steadiness in staying away from what He forbade, and steadiness under what He decrees. The Qur'an pairs it with prayer as the two things to seek help by (Qur'an 2:153). It does not mean feeling nothing: the Prophet peace be upon him wept when his son died and said the eye weeps and the heart grieves, but we say only what pleases our Lord, in Bukhari.

short: Gratitude that shows: knowing the gift, saying so, and using it as its Giver would like.
long: The Qur'an promises increase to those who are grateful (Qur'an 14:7). Scholars describe shukr working in three places at once: the heart admits where the gift came from, the tongue says it, and the limbs do not use the gift against the One who gave it. The Prophet peace be upon him also said that whoever does not thank people has not thanked Allah, in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi.

short: Relying on Allah for the outcome while still doing the work that leads to it.
long: The Qur'an says whoever relies on Allah, He is enough for him (Qur'an 65:3), and it also tells the Prophet peace be upon him to consult, then decide, then rely (Qur'an 3:159). When a man asked whether to leave his camel loose and trust Allah, he was told to tie it and then trust, in a report collected by Tirmidhi. Tawakkul is the state of the heart after you have done what you can, not a reason to do nothing.

short: Contentment with what Allah decrees, so the heart stops arguing with what already happened.
long: The word means to be pleased, and it runs both ways: Allah pleased with the believer and the believer pleased with Him (Qur'an 98:8). Scholars distinguish it from sabr, which holds steady under a blow, while rida no longer wishes the blow away. It applies to what has already been decreed. It does not mean accepting oppression, and it does not stop anyone from seeking a remedy.

short: Fear of Allah: the awareness of His justice that keeps a person from walking off the edge.
long: The Qur'an describes believers as those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned (Qur'an 8:2), and as calling on their Lord in fear and hope together (Qur'an 32:16). Scholars say the two wings must stay even: fear alone tips into despair, hope alone tips into carelessness. Healthy khawf is measured by what it makes you do, not by how bad it makes you feel.

short: Hope in Allah's mercy, held by someone who is still working, not by someone who has stopped.
long: The Qur'an forbids despair of Allah's mercy and says He forgives all sins (Qur'an 39:53). Scholars separate raja' from wishful thinking, tamanni: hope plants and then expects a crop, wishing expects a crop with no seed. A common counsel is to keep fear slightly ahead while a person is in health, and to keep hope ahead when death is near.

short: Love of Allah, measured less by what it feels like and more by what it follows.
long: The Qur'an says those who believe are strongest in love of Allah (Qur'an 2:165), and gives the test plainly: if you love Allah, follow the Messenger, and Allah will love you (Qur'an 3:31). Its signs are usually listed as preferring what He loves over what you want, ease in remembering Him, and love for the people who love Him. Sufi writers dwell on this station at length, but it is not a Sufi invention. It is in the verse.

short: The heart's stillness and lowering before Allah, of which focus in prayer is one part.
long: The Qur'an asks whether the time has not come for the hearts of the believers to soften at the remembrance of Allah (Qur'an 57:16), which is khushu' outside the prayer as well as inside it. It is closer to a lowering than to an emotion: the heart stops standing up straight in front of its Lord. For khushu' specifically during salah, see the separate entry under worship.

short: Remembrance of Allah, in set phrases and in the wider habit of not forgetting Him.
long: The Qur'an says hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah (Qur'an 13:28) and tells believers to remember Him and He will remember them (Qur'an 2:152). In practice dhikr covers the short phrases such as subhan Allah and la ilaha illa Allah, the morning and evening adhkar, reciting the Qur'an, and the wider state of living aware of Him. Sufi orders add group and audible forms, and that is where scholars disagree about method, not about dhikr itself.

short: Asking Allah directly, in any language, at any time, for anything permitted.
long: The Qur'an says call on Me and I will answer you (Qur'an 40:60), and the Prophet peace be upon him said du'a is worship itself, in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi. Scholars describe three possible answers: the thing asked for, something equal or better kept back for later, or a harm turned away. He also warned against impatience, saying a servant is answered as long as he does not say I asked and was not answered, in Bukhari and Muslim.

short: Asking Allah for forgiveness, usually in the words astaghfirullah.
long: The Qur'an links it to relief and provision, quoting Nuh telling his people to seek forgiveness of their Lord (Qur'an 71:10). The Prophet peace be upon him, already promised forgiveness for what preceded and what would follow (Qur'an 48:2), said he sought forgiveness a hundred times a day, in Muslim. Istighfar is the request; tawbah is the turn. They are usually done together, though a person can ask for pardon before they have managed to leave the sin.

short: Turning back to Allah from a sin: stopping it, regretting it, and resolving not to return.
long: The Qur'an calls for a sincere turning, tawbatan nasuha (Qur'an 66:8). Scholars list the conditions as leaving the sin, regretting it, resolving not to repeat it, and, where a person's right was taken, returning it or seeking their pardon. The Prophet peace be upon him said every child of Adam errs, and the best of those who err are those who repent, in a report collected by Tirmidhi. Falling again does not cancel the earlier repentance; it calls for another one.

short: Turning to Allah as a settled direction of life, not only as a return after one sin.
long: The Qur'an commands, turn to your Lord and submit to Him (Qur'an 39:54). Writers on the heart place inabah a step past tawbah: tawbah leaves a wrong behind, inabah keeps facing Him afterwards, in ease as well as in trouble. The picture in the root is of returning again and again to the same place.

short: Taking account of yourself: a regular, honest review of what you did and why.
long: The Qur'an tells each soul to look at what it has sent ahead for tomorrow (Qur'an 59:18), and a well known saying attributed to Umar ibn al-Khattab is to call yourselves to account before you are called to account. Scholars describe it as a short daily session rather than a long anxious one, done before the deed to check the intention and after it to check the result. It is a tool, and like any tool a scrupulous person can overuse it.

short: Living with the awareness that Allah sees you, at the moment you are acting.
long: The Qur'an says He is nearer to a person than his jugular vein (Qur'an 50:16), and that He is ever a watcher over you (Qur'an 4:1). It is the practical side of ihsan as the Prophet peace be upon him defined it to Jibril: worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then He sees you, in Bukhari and Muslim. Muhasabah looks back at the deed. Muraqabah stands inside it.

short: Holding the world loosely: having a thing in your hand without letting it into your heart.
long: The Prophet peace be upon him told a man to be indifferent to the world and Allah would love him, and to be indifferent to what people own and people would love him, in a report collected by Ibn Majah. Scholars are clear that zuhd is not poverty and not refusing what is lawful; several Companions were wealthy. It is the willingness to lose a thing without losing yourself along with it.

short: Caution that leaves what is unclear, in order to stay safe from what is forbidden.
long: The Prophet peace be upon him said the lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters, and whoever avoids them has protected his religion, in Bukhari and Muslim. He also said to leave what makes you uneasy for what does not, in a report collected by Tirmidhi. Wara' works one step further out than taqwa, in the grey band. It becomes a problem only when it turns into suspicion of everything and everyone.

short: Being satisfied with enough, so that what you do not have stops taking up room.
long: The Prophet peace be upon him said a person has succeeded who submitted, was given just enough, and was made content by Allah with what He gave him, in Muslim. He also said richness is not having many possessions, but richness of the soul, in Bukhari and Muslim. Qana'ah is not a ban on ambition or on earning. It is the removal of the ache that no amount answers.

short: Forbearance: the strength to stay calm and unhurried when you have every right to react.
long: The Prophet peace be upon him told al-Ashajj of Abd al-Qays that he had two qualities Allah loves, hilm and unhurriedness, in Muslim. The Qur'an describes the answer to a rough word as repelling with what is better (Qur'an 41:34). Hilm is not weakness and it is not indifference. The person is fully able to strike back and takes the slower road.

short: Pardon: dropping a wrong you are owed, without the other person having to earn it.
long: The Qur'an asks whether you would not love Allah to forgive you, in the middle of telling a wronged man to pardon (Qur'an 24:22), and says the reward of the one who pardons and reconciles is with Allah (Qur'an 42:40). Scholars distinguish 'afw, letting the debt go, from safh, letting the resentment go with it. The Prophet peace be upon him said Allah only increases a servant in honour for pardoning, in Muslim.

short: Mercy: the disposition to spare, relieve and be gentle, in Allah first and in people after.
long: The Qur'an says His mercy encompasses all things (Qur'an 7:156), and that the Prophet peace be upon him was sent as a mercy to the worlds (Qur'an 21:107). He said the merciful are shown mercy by the Most Merciful, and told his companions to be merciful to those on earth so that the One in the heaven would be merciful to them, in a report collected by Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi. Rahmah in a person is not softness of opinion. It is the reflex to relieve someone when you could have walked past.

short: Good manner in a specific situation: the right way to sit, speak, eat, enter, and ask.
long: Where akhlaq names the character underneath, adab names the outward form it takes here and now, and most of it was taught by example. Classical scholars wrote whole books on it, such as al-Bukhari's al-Adab al-Mufrad. Some adab is fixed by the Sunnah, such as eating with the right hand, and some varies with place and custom, which is why a practice can be good manners in one country and odd in another.

short: Character: the settled dispositions a person acts from before they have time to think.
long: The Qur'an describes the Prophet peace be upon him as being upon a great character (Qur'an 68:4), and he said he was sent to complete good character, in a report from Imam Ahmad. He also said the most complete believers in faith are the best of them in character, in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi. Scholars hold that character can be trained, which is the whole reason tazkiyah exists. Nobody is stuck with the temper they were born with.

short: A modesty that makes a person shrink from what is ugly, before Allah and before people.
long: The Prophet peace be upon him said modesty is a branch of faith, in Bukhari and Muslim, and that modesty brings nothing but good, in Muslim. It is a restraint that works before the act rather than a regret afterwards. It is not shyness of speech: a person can be modest and still ask a direct question, and the women of the Ansar were praised because shyness did not stop them learning their religion.

short: Soundness of the chest: carrying no grudge against anyone, whether or not they deserved one.
long: The Qur'an teaches the believers to pray that Allah leave no rancour in their hearts toward those who believed (Qur'an 59:10), and describes the people of Paradise as having every trace of it removed from their chests (Qur'an 7:43). In a report collected by Ahmad, a man was named as one of the people of Paradise, and the only practice found in him was that he went to sleep holding nothing against any Muslim. Forgiving the person is 'afw; salamat al-sadr is what remains in you afterwards.

short: Lying: saying what you know is not so, in speech, in a hint, or in a misleading silence.
long: The Prophet peace be upon him said truthfulness leads to righteousness and lying leads to wickedness, and a man keeps lying until he is written with Allah as a liar, in Bukhari and Muslim. He named lying among the signs of hypocrisy in conduct. Scholars allow a narrow room for concealment in order to reconcile people, to protect life, and between spouses, and even there the classical preference is to use words that are true but indirect.

short: Mentioning something about a person, behind their back, that they would dislike hearing.
long: The Qur'an compares it to eating the flesh of your dead brother (Qur'an 49:12). When the Prophet peace be upon him was asked what if it is true, he answered that if it is true you have backbitten him, and if it is not you have slandered him, in Muslim. Scholars list narrow exceptions, such as warning someone about a business partner or a marriage proposal, or reporting a wrong to a person able to stop it. These exist for need, not for cover.

short: Carrying words between people in a way that sets them against each other.
long: The Prophet peace be upon him said the one who carries tales will not enter Paradise, in Bukhari and Muslim, and he passed two graves whose occupants were being punished, one of them for namimah. The Qur'an condemns the one who goes about with slander (Qur'an 68:11). It differs from ghibah in its aim: ghibah damages a reputation, namimah damages a relationship.

short: Thinking well of people: reading an ambiguous act in the best way it can honestly be read.
long: The Qur'an tells believers to avoid much suspicion, and forbids spying and backbiting in the same verse (Qur'an 49:12). The Prophet peace be upon him said beware of suspicion, for suspicion is the most untruthful of speech, in Bukhari and Muslim. It does not require ignoring evidence or leaving yourself unprotected; it governs the gap where you do not actually know. The phrase is also used for thinking well of Allah, which the Sunnah treats as its own subject.

short: Envy: wishing a blessing would leave someone, rather than wishing you had one too.
long: The Qur'an teaches seeking refuge from the evil of an envier when he envies (Qur'an 113:5). Scholars separate blameworthy hasad, which wants the gift removed, from ghibtah, which wants the same gift without wanting anyone stripped of theirs; the second is permitted and even praised. Envy arrives without permission. What is judged is whether a person acts on it or feeds it.

short: Arrogance: rejecting the truth when you hear it, and looking down on people.
long: That is the Prophet's own definition, peace be upon him, given in Muslim when a man asked whether liking good clothes counted as arrogance. He answered that Allah is beautiful and loves beauty, then gave the two signs. The Qur'an warns against walking the earth in self-importance (Qur'an 31:18). Kibr is measured by what you do with a correction, not by what you wear.

short: Self-admiration: being impressed by your own good deed as though you produced it alone.
long: The Qur'an tells people not to claim purity for themselves (Qur'an 53:32). Scholars distinguish it from kibr: kibr needs someone to look down on, while 'ujb only needs a mirror. It is treated by remembering that the ability, the opportunity and the guidance were all given, and by noticing how quickly a deed you are proud of stops feeling sincere.

short: Humility: knowing your size, without pretending to be smaller than you are.
long: The Prophet peace be upon him said nobody humbles himself for Allah except that Allah raises him, in Muslim, and the Qur'an describes the servants of the Most Merciful as those who walk on the earth gently (Qur'an 25:63). Scholars define it as accepting the truth from whoever brings it, and not seeing yourself as above anyone. Performed modesty, staged so that people will admire it, belongs with riya rather than with tawadu'.

short: Anger, which is not a sin in itself, and is judged by what a person does while holding it.
long: A man asked the Prophet peace be upon him for advice and was told, do not become angry, and the man kept asking and got the same answer, in Bukhari. He also said the strong man is not the wrestler, but the one who controls himself when angry, in Bukhari and Muslim. The practical instructions include seeking refuge from Shaytan and sitting down if you are standing, in a report collected by Abu Dawud. The Qur'an praises those who restrain anger and pardon people (Qur'an 3:134), which is restraint, not absence.

short: Whispering: unwanted thoughts thrown at the heart, whether by Shaytan or by the mind itself.
long: The last surah of the Qur'an names the whisperer who whispers in the chests of people (Qur'an 114:4-5). The Prophet peace be upon him said Allah has pardoned this community for what their souls whisper as long as they do not act on it or speak it, in Bukhari and Muslim, and he taught that a person struck by doubts about creation should say I believe in Allah and move on. Distressing repetitive doubt about wudu, prayer or belief is a recognised condition, and treating it as a medical matter as well as a spiritual one is not a failure of faith.

short: Heedlessness: not the denial of the truth, but the habit of never getting round to it.
long: The Qur'an says people's reckoning has drawn near while they turn away heedless (Qur'an 21:1), and describes the heedless as further astray than cattle (Qur'an 7:179). It is the ordinary condition that dhikr exists to interrupt, which is one reason the adhkar are attached to times of day rather than to moods. Ghaflah is rarely a decision. It is what happens by default.

short: Hardness of heart: the state in which reminders arrive and nothing moves.
long: The Qur'an says hearts hardened after that until they were like stones or harder (Qur'an 2:74), and warns those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah (Qur'an 39:22). Classical writers trace it to accumulated small sins, idle talk, overeating, and long neglect of remembrance. The prescription they give is unglamorous: return to the daily adhkar, sit with people who remember Allah, visit the sick, and give something away.

short: Major sins: the ones the texts single out with a punishment, a curse, or a warning of the Fire.
long: The Qur'an promises that if you avoid the major sins you are forbidden, the smaller ones will be covered over (Qur'an 4:31). The Prophet peace be upon him named seven destructive sins in Bukhari and Muslim, among them shirk, killing a soul unjustly, and consuming interest. Scholars differ over the exact definition and therefore over the count, with classical books listing anywhere from seven to seventy and beyond. Minor sins turn serious when a person settles into them without concern.

short: Doubtful matters: the grey band between what is clearly lawful and what is clearly forbidden.
long: The Prophet peace be upon him said the lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are unclear matters that many people do not know, and whoever guards against them has protected his religion and his honour, in Bukhari and Muslim. The same hadith ends by naming the heart as the organ that settles the body. Leaving the doubtful is wara', and it is personal caution rather than a ruling you impose on other people.

short: Whim: personal desire raised high enough that a person follows it instead of the evidence.
long: The Qur'an asks whether you have seen the one who has taken his desire as his god (Qur'an 45:23), and promises the Garden to whoever feared standing before his Lord and restrained the self from its whim (Qur'an 79:40-41). It is used for appetite, but also for opinion held out of preference, which is why the early scholars called sects the people of desires. The test is what you do when the proof turns out to go against what you wanted.

short: Lowering the gaze: turning your eyes away from what you are not permitted to look at.
long: The Qur'an instructs believing men, and then believing women, to lower their gaze and guard their chastity (Qur'an 24:30-31). The Prophet peace be upon him told Ali that the first look is his and the second is not, in a report collected by Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi. Classical scholars treat it as the practical gate of the heart, on the principle that whatever the eye brings in, the heart has to carry. It is a discipline of the second look, not an order to walk with your head down.

short: The struggle against your own self: making yourself do the right thing when you do not want to.
long: The Qur'an promises guidance to those who strive for His sake (Qur'an 29:69). Classical writers describe it as three moves: opposing the appetite, refusing the whisper, and putting the limbs through the act until it becomes a habit. The often quoted line about returning from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad was judged by hadith scholars to have no sound chain, which does not remove the idea itself, since sound texts state it in other words.

short: Staying straight: keeping to the path steadily, over years, without dramatic swings.
long: When a man asked for a statement he would not need to ask anyone else about, the Prophet peace be upon him said, say I believe in Allah, then be upright, in Muslim. The Qur'an promises that angels descend on those who say our Lord is Allah and then remain steadfast (Qur'an 41:30). He also said the deeds most beloved to Allah are the most constant, even if they are few, in Bukhari and Muslim, which is the shape istiqamah usually takes in practice.

short: Deliberate reflection on creation and on your own life, treated as an act of worship.
long: The Qur'an describes people of understanding as those who remember Allah standing, sitting and lying on their sides, and who reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth (Qur'an 3:190-191). Scholars direct tafakkur outward at what has been made, and inward at one's own conduct, rather than at the nature of Allah Himself, which the mind cannot hold. A short honest stretch of thinking counts for more than a long distracted one.

short: Certainty: knowledge that has settled to the point where doubt no longer disturbs it.
long: The Qur'an mentions degrees that scholars read as a ladder: the knowledge of certainty and the eye of certainty (Qur'an 102:5-7), and the truth of certainty (Qur'an 56:95). The difference is like being told about a fire, then seeing it, then feeling its heat. The Qur'an also says worship your Lord until certainty comes to you (Qur'an 15:99), which the commentators explain as death.

short: A stillness Allah sends down into the heart, usually at the moment it is least expected.
long: The Qur'an says He sent down tranquillity into the hearts of the believers (Qur'an 48:4), and describes it arriving in the cave when the Prophet peace be upon him told Abu Bakr not to grieve (Qur'an 9:40). It is spoken of as given rather than produced. It is not the same as being calm by temperament, and its absence in a hard moment is not a sign that a person has been abandoned.

short: The opening of the chest: the settled ease Allah gives when a person is guided toward something.
long: The Qur'an says whoever Allah wishes to guide, He opens his chest to Islam (Qur'an 6:125), and reminds the Prophet peace be upon him that his own chest was opened for him (Qur'an 94:1). This is the usual answer to what happens after salat al-istikharah: not a dream and not a sign, but a decision that stops feeling stuck, followed by acting on it. If no clarity comes, you consult, you weigh, you choose, and you trust the outcome you are given.

short: The nearer life: this world, which is not condemned in itself, only when it becomes the whole aim.
long: The word means the nearer or the lower, and names this life set against the one that comes after. The Qur'an describes it as play, amusement and mutual boasting (Qur'an 57:20), and elsewhere tells a man not to forget his share of it. What is criticised is preferring it (Qur'an 87:16-17), not eating well, working, or loving your family. A useful reading: dunya is not the place, it is the place taken as final.

short: Generosity: giving easily, before being asked, without making the receiver pay in dignity.
long: The Qur'an says whoever is protected from the greed of his own soul, those are the successful (Qur'an 59:9), and the Prophet peace be upon him was described as the most generous of people, and most generous of all in Ramadan, in Bukhari and Muslim. Scholars place sakha' between two failures: miserliness on one side, wasteful display on the other. The measure in the Sunnah is what remains with you after the giving, not the size of what was given.

short: Companionship: the people you sit with, treated in the sources as a cause of what you become.
long: The Prophet peace be upon him compared a good companion to a seller of musk and a bad one to a blacksmith's bellows, in Bukhari and Muslim, and said a person follows the way of his close friend, in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi. Writers on the heart therefore treat the choice of company as an act with consequences rather than an accident. In Sufi usage suhbah also names the particular bond between a student and a teacher.

short: Sincere advice: wanting good for someone and telling them, privately and without an audience.
long: The Prophet peace be upon him said the religion is nasihah, and when asked to whom, said to Allah, to His Book, to His Messenger, to the leaders of the Muslims and to their common people, in Muslim. The word is wider than correction; it means genuine goodwill in what you say and in what you hold back. Classical scholars insisted that advice delivered in public is closer to shaming than to advising.

short: The set remembrances of the day: morning, evening, sleeping, waking, eating, travel and distress.
long: These are supplications the Prophet peace be upon him taught for particular moments, gathered in works such as al-Nawawi's al-Adhkar and, in our time, Hisn al-Muslim. Attaching remembrance to fixed times rather than to feelings is what allows it to survive a bad week. The wording is best kept as it was narrated, and the strength of the reports varies, so reliable collections mark which ones are authentic.

short: Declaring Allah free of every imperfection, most often in the words subhan Allah.
long: The Prophet peace be upon him said two phrases are light on the tongue and heavy on the scale, subhan Allah wa bihamdih and subhan Allah al-azim, in Bukhari and Muslim, and he taught the counts said before sleeping. He counted on his fingers and told the women to do the same, since the fingers will be asked to testify, in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi. Counting with beads was not the practice of his time; most later scholars allowed it as a tool, while some regarded it as an unwarranted addition.

short: Asking Allah to honour the Prophet, usually in the words sall Allahu alayhi wa sallam.
long: The Qur'an says Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet, and instructs the believers to do the same (Qur'an 33:56). He said, peace be upon him, that whoever sends one blessing upon him, Allah sends ten upon that person, in Muslim. The fullest wording is the one taught inside the tashahhud, known as the Ibrahimic form. Elaborate composed litanies of salawat circulate in some traditions, and scholars differ on using them in place of the narrated wording.

short: A personal daily portion of remembrance or recitation that a person keeps to.
long: The word means a turn at a watering place. In practice a wird is a small fixed amount, a page of Qur'an, a number of salawat, a set of adhkar, repeated every day at the same point. The principle behind it is the prophetic teaching that the deeds most loved by Allah are the constant ones, even if small. Sufi orders assign a specific wird through a shaykh; outside that setting a person simply chooses their own and keeps it.

short: The Islamic tradition of inner purification, called Sufism in English, and read very differently by different scholars.
long: At its origin the word names the science of the heart: sincerity, remembrance, character and struggle against the self, as taught by early figures such as al-Junayd and later organised by al-Ghazali. Over the centuries it also grew orders, practices and claims that other scholars judged to be innovations, and opinion today runs from full acceptance to full rejection, with many holding the content sound wherever it stays inside the Book and the Sunnah. When you meet the word it helps to ask which is meant: the subject matter, or a particular order and what it does.

short: A Sufi order: a lineage with a shaykh, a set litany, and a method for training students.
long: The word means path. Well known orders include the Qadiriyyah, the Naqshbandiyyah, the Shadhiliyyah and the Chishtiyyah, each with its own wird and manners. Belonging to one has never been a requirement in Islam, and scholars differ sharply about the orders as institutions, some treating them as a school of character, others objecting to particular practices found within them. The word is not used in this sense outside Sufi circles.

short: A station on the spiritual path, in the vocabulary used mainly by Sufi writers.
long: In that literature a maqam is a stage the traveller reaches and holds by effort, such as repentance, patience or reliance, while a hal is a state that comes over the heart and passes, such as a moment of intense longing. The lists and their order differ from author to author. Outside Sufi writing the same qualities are discussed without this ranking.

short: Blessing: a quality Allah puts in a thing so that a small amount goes further than it should.
long: The Qur'an speaks of blessings opened from the sky and the earth for a town that believes (Qur'an 7:96), and quotes Isa saying he was made blessed wherever he is (Qur'an 19:31). Barakah attaches to time, food, wealth, knowledge and people, and it is not measured in quantity: an hour with barakah does the work of three. The Sunnah connects it with naming Allah before eating, honesty in trade, early mornings, and gratitude.

short: Seeking blessing through a person, place or object, which scholars permit narrowly and dispute widely.
long: The Companions sought blessing through the person of the Prophet peace be upon him, his hair and the water left from his wudu, which is established in Bukhari and Muslim. Everyone agrees that the blessing itself comes from Allah alone. Scholars disagree about extending the practice after his death to graves, relics and living righteous people, some permitting it within limits, others treating it as a door that opens onto shirk. All sides agree that asking the object itself for anything is not tabarruk but worship of it.

short: Reciting Qur'an and prophetic supplications over a sick or afflicted person as treatment.
long: The Qur'an calls itself a healing for what is in the chests (Qur'an 10:57). The Prophet peace be upon him permitted ruqya so long as it contains no shirk, in Muslim, and approved a Companion who recited al-Fatihah over a man who had been stung, in Bukhari and Muslim. Anyone may recite over themselves or their family; no special person is required. Large fees, secret formulas, unintelligible words, and requests for the patient's mother's name are all signs to walk away.

short: The last two surahs of the Qur'an, al-Falaq and al-Nas, recited for protection.
long: The Prophet peace be upon him said verses had been revealed the like of which had never been seen, and then recited these two, in Muslim. He blew into his hands with them and with al-Ikhlas before sleeping and wiped over his body, in Bukhari, and taught that reciting the three surahs morning and evening suffices a person against everything, in a report collected by Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi. They are the core of any ruqya, and a person says them over themselves without needing a specialist.

short: The evil eye: real harm that can follow an admiring or an envious look.
long: The Prophet peace be upon him said the eye is true, in Bukhari and Muslim, and in a report in Malik's Muwatta he instructed a man whose look had harmed another to wash, and the water was poured over the one affected. It can come from someone who wishes you no harm at all, which is why the Sunnah answer is to ask Allah to bless what you admire. Treatment is ruqya and the prophetic supplications. It is not a reason to hide your life or to start suspecting your neighbours.

short: Sorcery: real in its effect, but powerless to harm anyone except by Allah's permission.
long: The word covers sorcery worked with the help of devils, and the Qur'an describes it plainly while making clear that it harms nobody except by Allah's permission (Qur'an 2:102). The Prophet peace be upon him was himself affected by it, in Bukhari and Muslim, and he recovered; he also named it among the seven destructive sins. Learning it or commissioning it is a grave matter, and the schools of law differ over the penalty for the one who practises it. The treatment is ruqya, the daily adhkar and ordinary medicine, never counter-magic.

short: Undoing magic with magic, which the Sunnah rejects, unlike undoing it with the Qur'an.
long: Asked about nushrah, the Prophet peace be upon him said it is from the work of Shaytan, in a report collected by Abu Dawud. Scholars read this as the pre-Islamic method of going to another practitioner to break a spell, and they distinguish it from ruqya with the Qur'an and lawful supplication, which is permitted and was done by the Companions. In practice this is the line between a healer who recites what you can hear and understand, and one who does not.

short: Jinn touch: the claim that a jinn can affect, or enter, a human being.
long: The Qur'an describes a man rising as one struck by the touch of Shaytan (Qur'an 2:275), and the majority of Sunni scholars, Ibn Taymiyyah among them, took the possibility as established, while a minority read the verse as an image rather than a report. Even among those who affirm it, the classical books warn that most cases brought to them turned out to be illness, hardship or imagination. Where the symptoms are physical or psychiatric, the ordinary duty to seek medical treatment is not suspended.

short: An amulet worn for protection, whose ruling depends on what has been put inside it.
long: Amulets containing the names of jinn, unknown words or symbols are forbidden by agreement, and the Prophet peace be upon him warned that whoever hangs an amulet has been left to it, in reports collected by Ahmad and Tirmidhi. Amulets containing Qur'an are where scholars part company: Ibn Mas'ud and many after him prohibited them without distinction, while Abdullah ibn Amr and a number of Malikis and Shafi'is allowed the Qur'anic kind. Both sides agree the protection is from Allah, not from the paper.

short: Cupping: suction on the skin with small incisions to draw blood out, practised and praised by the Prophet.
long: He was cupped, peace be upon him, and said that among the best of the remedies people use is cupping, in reports collected by Bukhari and Muslim. It is a recommended treatment, not an act of worship and not a cure for everything, and the reports naming particular days of the month are weighed differently by different scholars. It should be done by someone trained and clean. It is medicine, and the ordinary rules of medicine apply to it.
